notes.summary: Probability measures how likely an event is, on a scale from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). Paper 2 asks about the three definitions (classical, relative frequency, axiomatic), counting outcomes with combinations, the addition and multiplication rules, conditional probability, independence, and Bayes' theorem. Most questions are short calculations with coins, dice, cards and balls in a bag.

concepts.title: Basic words
concepts.body:
• Random experiment: an action whose result cannot be predicted in advance, such as tossing a coin.
  • Sample space (S): the set of all possible outcomes. Tossing one coin: S = {H, T}. Throwing one die: S = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}.
  • Event: any subset of S. "Even number on a die" = {2, 4, 6}.
  • Equally likely: no outcome is more likely than another (a fair coin or die).
  • Mutually exclusive: the events cannot happen together, so A∩B = ∅. Getting 1 and getting 6 on one throw.
  • Exhaustive: together the events cover the whole sample space, so A∪B∪… = S.
  • Complement A′ (or Ac): "A does not happen". P(A′) = 1 − P(A).
  • Independent: one event happening does not change the chance of the other.

concepts.title: Three definitions of probability
concepts.body:
DefinitionRuleLimitation
Classical (a priori, Laplace)P(A) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomesNeeds a finite number of equally likely outcomes
Relative frequency (empirical, von Mises)P(A) = limit of (times A happened ÷ number of trials) as trials grow very largeNeeds the experiment to be repeated many times under the same conditions
Axiomatic (Kolmogorov)Any rule P that obeys the three axioms belowDoes not tell you how to find the actual value

Kolmogorov's axioms:

  1. P(A) ≥ 0 for every event A.
  2. P(S) = 1.
  3. For mutually exclusive A1, A2, …: P(A1∪A2∪…) = P(A1) + P(A2) + …

From these follow: P(∅) = 0, 0 ≤ P(A) ≤ 1, and P(A′) = 1 − P(A).

concepts.body:

One die63 even, 3 odd, 3 primes (2, 3, 5)

Example: two dice, P(sum = 7) = 6/36 = 1/6, the most likely sum.

concepts.title: Counting with combinations
concepts.body:
When several items are drawn together (or one by one without caring about order), count with combinations: nCr = n! ÷ (r! (n − r)!).

  • nC0 = nCn = 1, nC1 = n, nCr = nCn−r.
  • 5C2 = 10, 8C2 = 28, 52C2 = 1326.

Example: a bag has 4 red and 6 white balls. Two are drawn. P(one of each) = (4C1 × 6C1) ÷ 10C2 = 24/45 = 8/15.

concepts.title: Addition rule
concepts.body:
• Any two events: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). We subtract the overlap because it was counted twice.
  • Mutually exclusive: P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B).
  • Three events: P(A∪B∪C) = ΣP(A) − ΣP(A∩B) + P(A∩B∩C).
  • "Only A" = P(A) − P(A∩B). "Exactly one" = P(A) + P(B) − 2P(A∩B).
  • "Neither" = 1 − P(A∪B) (De Morgan: (A∪B)′ = A′∩B′).

Example: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4, P(A∩B) = 0.2. P(A∪B) = 0.7, P(neither) = 0.3, P(exactly one) = 0.5.

concepts.title: Conditional probability and multiplication rule
concepts.body:
• P(A|B) = P(A∩B) ÷ P(B), the chance of A once we know B has happened (P(B) > 0).
  • Multiplication rule: P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B|A) = P(B) × P(A|B).
  • Drawing without replacement changes the second probability. Two aces from 52 cards: (4/52) × (3/51) = 1/221.
  • Drawing with replacement keeps it the same: (4/52) × (4/52) = 1/169.

concepts.title: Independent events
concepts.body:
• A and B are independent if P(A∩B) = P(A) × P(B), which is the same as P(A|B) = P(A).
  • If A, B are independent, so are A and B′, A′ and B, A′ and B′.
  • P(at least one) = 1 − P(A′) × P(B′). P(neither) = P(A′) × P(B′).
  • Independent is not the same as mutually exclusive. Two mutually exclusive events with non-zero probability can never be independent, because P(A∩B) = 0 but P(A)P(B) > 0.
  • Three events are mutually independent only if every pair and the triple satisfy the product rule.

Example: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5, independent. P(both) = 0.3, P(neither) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2, P(at least one) = 0.8.

concepts.title: Total probability and Bayes' theorem
concepts.body:
Let E1, E2, …, En be mutually exclusive and exhaustive (for example, which machine made an item).

  • Total probability: P(A) = Σ P(Ei) P(A|Ei).
  • Bayes' theorem: P(Ei|A) = P(Ei) P(A|Ei) ÷ Σ P(Ej) P(A|Ej).
  • P(Ei) are prior probabilities; P(Ei|A) are posterior probabilities.
MachineShareDefective rateProduct
A0.60.020.012
B0.40.030.012
Total0.024

P(A | defective) = 0.012 ÷ 0.024 = 0.5.

concepts.title: Odds
concepts.body:
• Odds in favour of A = P(A) : P(A′) = favourable : unfavourable.
  • Odds against A = P(A′) : P(A).
  • If odds in favour are a : b, then P(A) = a ÷ (a + b).

Example: odds against an event are 7 : 3, so P(event) = 3/10.

varieties.name: Coins, dice and cards
varieties.how: List or count the sample space, count the favourable outcomes, and divide. Use the complement for "at least one".

example.q: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum is 8?

varieties.name: Drawing with combinations
varieties.how: Favourable = product of <sup>n</sup>C<sub>r</sub> for each colour or group chosen; total = <sup>N</sup>C<sub>r</sub> for the whole draw.

example.q: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. Two balls are drawn at random. Find the probability that both are red.

varieties.name: Addition rule and complements
varieties.how: Use P(A∪B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A∩B). Drop the overlap term only if the events are mutually exclusive.

example.q: One card is drawn from a pack of 52. Find the probability that it is a king or a heart.
steps: The king of hearts is in both: P(both) = 1/52.

varieties.name: Conditional probability and independence
varieties.how: For "given that" use P(A|B) = P(A∩B)/P(B). For independent events multiply. Without replacement, reduce the counts for the second draw.

varieties.name: Total probability and Bayes' theorem
varieties.how: Make a table: prior × likelihood for each source. Add the products for the total; the wanted row's product ÷ total is the answer.

example.q: Urn I has 3 white and 2 black balls; urn II has 2 white and 3 black. An urn is chosen at random and a ball drawn is white. Find the probability that it came from urn I.

varieties.name: Definitions, axioms and odds
varieties.how: Match the words exactly: mutually exclusive means no overlap, exhaustive means they cover S, independent means the product rule holds. For odds a : b in favour, P = a/(a + b).

example.q: The odds in favour of an event are 3 : 5. What is its probability?

tips: "At least one" is almost always fastest as 1 − P(none).
Two dice: the number of ways to get sum s is 6 − |s − 7|.
Before using Bayes, check that the shares of the sources add to 1.
For independent events, P(at least one) = 1 − (1 − p<sub>1</sub>)(1 − p<sub>2</sub>)….
Probability is always between 0 and 1; any option outside this range can be struck off.
In Bayes questions the answer is usually a simple fraction once you clear the percentages.
traps: Mutually exclusive and independent are different ideas; do not use the product rule for mutually exclusive events.
Without replacement, the second draw has one item fewer in the total and possibly in the favourable count.
P(A|B) is not the same as P(B|A).
A pack has 12 face cards (J, Q, K); aces are not face cards.

formulas.name: Classical probability
formulas.expr: P(A) = favourable outcomes ÷ total equally likely outcomes

formulas.name: Odds
formulas.expr: Odds in favour a : b ⇒ P = a ÷ (a + b)

questions.q: Two fair coins are tossed. The probability of getting at least one head is:
questions.solution:
Outcomes: HH, HT, TH, TT. Only TT has no head.
P(at least one head) = 1 − 1/4 = 3/4.

questions.q: A fair die is thrown. The probability of getting a number greater than 4 is:
questions.solution:
Numbers greater than 4: 5 and 6, i.e. 2 out of 6.
P = 2/6 = 1/3.
